content: Devices are available and tailored to the specific requirements of the procedure. Evidence to guide recommendations on the use of device-based methods, including in-situ and surgical assistance, has been reviewed. Tim Farley, a statistician from Sigma3 Services, has contributed to the analysis of critical and important outcomes, including: Priority Outcomes: Critical: Eligibility criteria, including contraindications specific to the device method, in addition to standard exclusions for voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC). Efficacy, defined as successful circumcision using the device method alone. Safety, focusing on serious, severe, and moderate adverse events. Cosmetic outcomes of the procedure. Important: Procedure times. Acceptability, including cosmetic results and time required to return to normal daily activities. Pain experienced before, during, and after the circumcision procedure. Healing time. Odor associated with the device. Only circumcision devices with sufficient clinical data to be considered for the WHO Circumcision Device Prequalification process were included in the analysis. Published data were supplemented with clinical performance information submitted by manufacturers to WHO. Summary of Studies on Collar Clamp Devices: Study Types: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing collar clamp devices to surgical circumcision. Concurrent cohort studies. Findings: In RCTs, 263 clients (all aged ≥18 years) were studied in Kenya, Uganda, and Zambia. One study in China included 314 clients. Between 4% and 55% of 3,377 eligible men could not undergo circumcision with the collar clamp device due to the unavailability of the correct ring size at the clinic. Approximately 95% of men were successfully circumcised using the device alone. Moderate adverse events occurred in 3% of cases (14 out of 264), with 9 requiring sutures to control post-operative bleeding. The device produced neat, uniform circumferential wounds, with 90-95% fully healed by four weeks. Additional data are required on clinical performance under field conditions with a broader range of providers. Evidence Quality: In-situ Devices: Moderate quality evidence for use among males aged 15 years and older. Low-quality evidence for males aged 10-14 years. Surgical Assist Devices: Low-quality evidence. Collar Clamp Device Implementation: Implementation phases have been conducted in several African countries, including Kenya, Mozambique, Malawi, Namibia, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, Zimbabwe, and Zambia. These phases included training, pilot studies, and active and passive adverse event follow-up. Pilot studies (~500 clients) assessed whether the device is as safe, effective, and acceptable as in studies submitted for prequalification. Active adverse event follow-up (first ~1,000 clients) evaluated safety, effectiveness, and acceptability at scale. Passive adverse event follow-up (routine services) assessed safety, effectiveness, and acceptability during routine use. Acceptability of Device-Based Methods: High satisfaction rates with cosmetic results were reported among adult men and adolescent boys. Studies consistently found minimal interference with clients’ work or daily activities, though evidence was limited. Some clients reported bad odor while wearing elastic collar compression devices, but not with collar clamp devices. Device-based VMMC is generally acceptable among adult men and adolescent boys. Key Considerations: Healing time for in-situ placement devices is 1-2 weeks longer than for surgical circumcision. Counseling on a longer period of sexual abstinence is essential. Procedure times for device-based methods are shorter than for conventional surgery, including both placement and removal visits. Providers found the procedure easier to perform, which facilitated acceptability and better outcomes. Perspectives from female sexual partners, wider communities, policymakers, and funders remain unknown. Cost Implications: Costs for device-based VMMC vary depending on the type of device used. Consumables and staffing costs are significant contributors to total costs. Shorter procedure durations reduce clinician time costs, but device costs, associated medical supplies, and removal costs must be considered. Existing evidence primarily focuses on elastic compression and collar clamp in-situ devices. Limited data are available on the overall cost of device-based methods. Feasibility of Implementation: Evidence on constraints or barriers to implementing device-based methods is lacking. Limited VMMCs have been performed using devices, but feasibility has been high where they have been used, including allowing less surgically skilled providers to perform circumcisions. VMMC scale-up has largely been achieved with surgical methods. No evidence suggests barriers to the use of in-situ devices, though the requirement for tetanus toxoid (TT) vaccination for elastic collar compression devices limits their use.
